niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.title: Remember the point at infinity? Florence got there first.
niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.hook: Painters were drawing the point at infinity for two hundred years before a mathematician admitted it was a point.
niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.body:
In projective geometry you adjoin points at infinity so that parallel lines meet, and Euclidean geometry becomes a special case. It feels like a formal convenience invented to tidy up theorems.

It was invented by painters, and it was not a convenience — it was an observation. Sometime between 1415 and 1420 Filippo Brunelleschi ran a demonstration in Florence involving a painted panel of the Baptistery, a peephole drilled through it and a mirror, so a viewer could compare the painted building with the real one. By 1435 Leon Battista Alberti had written *De pictura*, setting out the construction: the parallel edges of a tiled floor converge to a single point on the horizon.

That point is not an artistic convention. It is where those parallel lines genuinely go. Girard Desargues (1591–1661), who knew the perspective literature, took it seriously and built the geometry — then was ignored so completely that his work survived through a handwritten copy Michel Chasles stumbled on in 1845.

Here is the correspondence, exactly.
niche.art.perspective-math.remember-the-.rigor:
Model the eye at the origin of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and the canvas as the plane $z=1$. A point $(x,y,z)$ with $z>0$ is painted at $(x/z,\,y/z)$ — which is precisely the map from $\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\}$ to homogeneous coordinates. A painting *is* a chart of $\mathbb{P}^{2}(\mathbb{R})$.

Take the ray through a scene point $p_0$ in direction $v$: $p(t)=p_0+tv$. Its image is

$$\frac{p_0+tv}{(p_0+tv)_z}\;\xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\;\frac{v}{v_z},$$

independent of $p_0$. That limit is the vanishing point, and the computation says the two things a painter knows by instinct: it depends only on the *direction* $v$, so all lines parallel to $v$ share one vanishing point; and a direction with $v_z=0$ — parallel to the canvas — has no vanishing point at all, which is why the verticals of a building stay parallel in a painting.

The set of vanishing points of all directions lying in a given plane is a line on the canvas. For the ground plane, that line is the horizon. The horizon is the line at infinity, and you have been looking at it your whole life.

recall.question: In a perspective painting, why do a building's vertical edges stay parallel while the road's edges converge?

options.text: The verticals are parallel to the picture plane, so their direction has no vanishing point
options.why: only directions with a component towards the viewer converge.

options.text: Because artists choose to draw them that way for balance
options.why: the construction is forced by the projection, not chosen.

options.text: Because vertical lines are infinitely long and horizontal ones are not
options.why: length is irrelevant; only direction relative to the canvas matters.

niche.food.coffee.caffeine-is-an-insecti.title: Your coffee is a plant's chemical weapon, badly aimed
niche.food.coffee.caffeine-is-an-insecti.hook: The coffee plant did not make caffeine for you. It made it to poison insects and sterilise the soil around itself.
niche.food.coffee.caffeine-is-an-insecti.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Softened the afternoon-crash mechanism from stated fact to the usual explanation.

niche.food.coffee.caffeine-is-an-insecti.body:
Caffeine is a defence molecule. It protects the coffee plant against herbivores, and it leaches into the soil where it suppresses the germination of competing seeds — the plant poisons its own neighbourhood to keep the space. Some plants also put small doses in their nectar, where it encourages the bees rather than repelling them.

We drink it. And here is the part that changes how you think about a cup: caffeine gives you nothing.

All day, your brain accumulates adenosine, a by-product that binds to receptors and produces the sensation of tiredness. Caffeine is shaped enough like adenosine to occupy those receptors without activating them. It does not add energy, or alertness, or capability. It sits in the doorway so the tiredness signal cannot get in.

The adenosine is still arriving the whole time. When the caffeine clears, all of it lands at once — which is the usual explanation for the afternoon crash.

recall.question: What does caffeine actually do in the brain?

options.text: It releases stored energy from glucose
options.why: caffeine supplies no energy and does not unlock any; the feeling of energy is the absence of a signal.

options.text: It blocks adenosine receptors without activating them, so the accumulating tiredness signal cannot be received
options.why: the adenosine keeps building up behind it.

options.text: It speeds up neuron firing directly
options.why: its primary action is receptor blockade, not direct excitation.

niche.food.coffee.juan-valdez-no-existe.title: El campesino más famoso del mundo nunca existió
niche.food.coffee.juan-valdez-no-existe.hook: Juan Valdez lo inventó una agencia de Nueva York en 1958. Fue la mejor política económica del café colombiano.
niche.food.coffee.juan-valdez-no-existe.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.food.coffee.juan-valdez-no-existe.body:
Un productor de materia prima no tiene precio propio: vende a lo que diga la bolsa de Nueva York. La Federación Nacional de Cafeteros, fundada el 27 de junio de 1927, entendió temprano la única salida posible: dejar de vender un commodity y empezar a vender una marca.

En 1958 la agencia Doyle Dane Bernbach inventó a Juan Valdez —sombrero, poncho, mula— con un objetivo estrecho y medible: que el consumidor estadounidense distinguiera el café 100% colombiano de las mezclas. Lo interpretaron tres actores en más de sesenta años, el más recordado Carlos Sánchez, entre 1969 y 2006. Ningún otro país cafetero logró nada parecido.

La prueba de para qué servía llegó el 4 de julio de 1989, cuando el Consejo Internacional del Café suspendió el sistema de cuotas de exportación que sostenía los precios desde 1962. El precio indicativo promedio pasó de 1,34 dólares por libra en el quinquenio anterior a 0,77 en el posterior: casi la mitad.

Cuando se cae el cartel, lo único que queda para defender el precio es que alguien prefiera tu grano por el nombre.

recall.question: ¿Por qué una marca como Juan Valdez es una decisión económica y no solo publicitaria?
recall.answer: Porque el productor de un commodity es tomador de precio: vende al precio internacional, sin margen propio. Diferenciar el producto —que el comprador pida café colombiano y no café— es la única forma de capturar un sobreprecio. Eso quedó a la vista en 1989, cuando se suspendieron las cuotas del pacto cafetero y el precio indicativo cayó de 1,34 a 0,77 dólares por libra.

sources.title: Federación Nacional de Cafeteros de Colombia

niche.games.chess-go.two-rules-and-no-en.title: A game you can teach in five minutes and lose at for fifty years
niche.games.chess-go.two-rules-and-no-en.hook: Go's rules fit on a postcard. The number of legal positions has 171 digits.
niche.games.chess-go.two-rules-and-no-en.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Go did not fall to brute force: AlphaGo won in 2016 with a neural network, not search. Corrected and trimmed to length.

niche.games.chess-go.two-rules-and-no-en.body:
Chess needs a page of rules: six pieces, each moving differently, plus castling, en passant and promotion. Go needs two. Stones are captured when they have no adjacent empty points left — no liberties. And you may not repeat a previous board position, which stops infinite loops. That is essentially it; the rest is turn order and how you count at the end.

From those two rules comes a 19-by-19 board with 361 points and roughly $2.1\times 10^{170}$ legal positions — more than the estimated number of atoms in the observable universe, by about ninety orders of magnitude. Every move offers hundreds of plausible options rather than chess's dozens, and games run far longer.

This is the interesting asymmetry: rule complexity and game complexity are almost unrelated. Tic-tac-toe has simple rules and a trivial game. Go has simpler rules than chess and a vastly larger game. What generates depth is not how much the rules say, but how much interaction they permit.

Which is why brute force beat Kasparov in 1997 and got nowhere here. Go fell in 2016, to a neural network that guessed at positions instead of counting them.

recall.question: What does Go's ko rule exist to prevent?

options.text: Endless repetition
options.why: it forbids recreating a previous board position, so capture-and-recapture cycles cannot loop forever.

options.text: Capturing large groups
options.why: group capture is exactly what the liberty rule is for and is entirely legal.

options.text: Playing on the edges of the board
options.why: edge points have fewer liberties but are perfectly legal to play.

niche.games.game-design.the-anti-landlor.title: The board game designed as propaganda against itself
niche.games.game-design.the-anti-landlor.hook: Monopoly was invented to teach you that landlords are the problem. It came with a second rule set nobody plays.
niche.games.game-design.the-anti-landlor.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Parker Brothers' token run of The Landlord's Game was 1939; sequencing corrected.

niche.games.game-design.the-anti-landlor.body:
In 1904 Elizabeth "Lizzie" Magie patented The Landlord's Game. She was a follower of Henry George, who argued that land rent enriches owners without their producing anything, and she built the board as an argument: go round, land on other people's property, pay, get poorer, watch one player end up with everything.

The design move that makes her a serious game designer is the second rule set. The same board could be played two ways. Under the monopolist rules you win by bankrupting everyone. Under the anti-monopolist rules, rents fed a common pot and every player got richer together. You played both, and the point was the comparison.

Parker Brothers bought Monopoly in the 1930s from Charles Darrow, who claimed to have invented it. In 1935 they bought Magie's patent too, for \$500, pushed her game aside within a year, and in 1939 printed a token run of it to secure the rights.

So the world's best-known board game is a teaching tool with its lesson removed — and the reason everyone finds Monopoly miserable and interminable is that it is *working exactly as designed*.

recall.question: What did Lizzie Magie's original 1904 game include that Monopoly does not?
recall.answer: A second, anti-monopolist rule set for the same board, in which rents went to a common pot and all players prospered together. Playing both versions was the point: the contrast was the argument for Henry George's land-value tax.

niche.language.etymology.nobody-was-paid.title: The salt in your salary is a rumour
niche.language.etymology.nobody-was-paid.hook: Salary really does come from the Latin for salt. Roman soldiers really were not paid in salt.
niche.language.etymology.nobody-was-paid.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.language.etymology.nobody-was-paid.body:
Everyone has heard it: legionaries were paid in salt, hence *salarium*, hence "worth his salt". Half of that is true. The Latin *salarium* is genuinely built on *sal*, salt — that part is not in doubt.

The practice is. No ancient source records soldiers being paid in salt, or even given a salt allowance; the claim that they were is described in reference works as baseless. What the money had to do with salt, nobody actually knows.

A word can preserve a connection perfectly and lose the reason for it entirely.

recall.question: Which half of the "paid in salt" story survives scrutiny?
recall.answer: The etymology. *Salarium* is built on *sal* (salt) — but no ancient source attests soldiers being paid in salt, or receiving a salt ration. The link is real; the explanation is folk history.

niche.language.etymology.two-words-from-.title: One man in Baghdad named two-thirds of your maths vocabulary
niche.language.etymology.two-words-from-.hook: Algebra is named after a book about setting broken bones. Algorithm is named after the man who wrote it.
niche.language.etymology.two-words-from-.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Softened an unverifiable superlative about the word 'algorithm'.

niche.language.etymology.two-words-from-.body:
Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī, working in Baghdad sometime between 813 and 833, wrote a book with *al-jabr* in the title. The word did not mean anything mathematical yet: *al-jabr* was what a surgeon did to a broken bone — forcing the parts back together. Al-Khwārizmī borrowed it for what you do to an equation when you move a term across the equals sign and make the pieces whole again.

Latin translators turned *al-jabr* into *algebra* and kept it.

Then they did it again with his name. Al-Khwārizmī also wrote the manual that taught Europe to calculate with Hindu–Arabic numerals instead of Roman ones, and the Latin versions open with *Algoritmi* — his name, mangled. The step-by-step method in the book took on the name of the man: *algorism*, eventually *algorithm*.

So every time you say "algorithm" you are mispronouncing a place name — al-Khwārizmī means "the man from Khwarazm", a region south of the Aral Sea. Twelve centuries later it is one of the most-used words in technology.

recall.question: Where do the words "algebra" and "algorithm" come from, and what did *al-jabr* originally mean?
recall.answer: Both trace to one 9th-century scholar. *Algebra* comes from *al-jabr* in the title of his book — a word that originally meant bone-setting, the forcing back together of broken parts. *Algorithm* comes from the Latinisation of his own name, *Algoritmi*.

niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.title: The one word almost every language agrees on
niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.hook: Ten unrelated languages, five continents, one nearly identical syllable for "I did not catch that".
niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.body:
Words are supposed to be arbitrary. *Dog*, *perro*, *inu* — no reason for any of them, which is why unrelated languages sound nothing alike. Then there is *huh?*

Mark Dingemanse, Francisco Torreira and N. J. Enfield recorded ordinary conversation in ten languages from five continents — Siwu in Ghana, Cha'palaa in Ecuador, Murriny Patha in Australia, Icelandic, Mandarin, Spanish — and found the same item in each: a short, questioning syllable, low front vowel, no consonants to speak of, rising intonation. Close enough that the similarity is far beyond chance.

Their explanation is not shared ancestry, and not instinct. It is convergent evolution. Every conversation on Earth faces the same engineering problem: you missed something, and you have a fraction of a second to say so before the speaker moves on. The solution has to be minimal — one syllable, producible with a half-open mouth, unmistakably a question. Selection pressure that specific yields the same shape everywhere.

And the second claim of the paper is the subtler one.
niche.language.linguistics.huh-is-everyw.rigor:
The authors argue *huh?* is a **word**, not a grunt, and the distinction is testable. A cry of pain or a sneeze is involuntary and its form is not language-specific. A word is conventional, learned, and fitted to the sound system of its language.

Their evidence: the vowel in *huh?* is not identical across languages but varies *within each language's own vowel inventory*, and the intonation follows the language's own question prosody — rising in English and Spanish, falling in Icelandic, where questions fall. A reflex would not be locally adapted like that. Children have to learn it.

So the argument is a two-sided one, and both sides matter: the *function* is universal because the interactional problem is universal, while the *form* is conventional because it has been fitted to each language. The similarity is not inheritance from a common ancestor but the same problem solved the same way, independently, thousands of times — the linguistic version of the eye evolving again and again.

recall.question: What is the evidence that *huh?* is a learned word rather than an involuntary noise?

options.text: It appears in every recorded language
options.why: universality is compatible with a reflex; sneezes are universal too.

options.text: Its vowel and intonation are fitted to each language's own sound system and question prosody
options.why: a reflex would not vary language by language in exactly that way.

options.text: It is written down in dictionaries
options.why: orthography reflects convention about spelling, not whether the item is linguistic.

sources.title: Is "Huh?" a Universal Word? Conversational Infrastructure and the Convergent Evolution of Linguistic Items
sources.author: Dingemanse, Torreira and Enfield

niche.language.spanish.el-abecedario-per.title: En 2010 el español perdió dos letras
niche.language.spanish.el-abecedario-per.hook: La RAE prometió en 1713 limpiar y fijar el idioma. Trescientos años después su mejor trabajo ha sido ceder.
niche.language.spanish.el-abecedario-per.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: 'Siglo y medio' was wrong: ch and ll were letters from the 1754 Ortografia until 2010.

niche.language.spanish.el-abecedario-per.body:
La *ch* y la *ll* fueron letras del abecedario desde la *Ortografía* de 1754. Ya no lo son. La *Ortografía de la lengua española* de 2010 las degradó a dígrafos: dos letras escritas juntas, como la *rr*. El abecedario quedó en veintisiete.

No fue un capricho. En 1994 las academias ya habían decidido ordenarlas dentro de la *c* y la *l* para alfabetizar como el resto del mundo latino, y en 2010 sacaron la conclusión: si no se ordenan aparte, no son letras aparte. Lo que no cambió fue la escritura. *Chocolate* sigue escribiéndose igual.

Lo interesante es quién decide. La Academia nació el 6 de julio de 1713, por iniciativa del marqués de Villena, con un lema de crisol y fuego: *limpia, fija y da esplendor*. Pero desde hace décadas no manda sola: la RAE y las otras veintitrés academias forman la ASALE, y las normas se pactan entre todas. Bogotá, Ciudad de México y Buenos Aires votan.

Una institución fundada para purificar terminó haciendo estadística descriptiva del uso.

recall.question: ¿Qué cambió exactamente en 2010 con la ch y la ll?

options.text: Dejaron de considerarse letras del abecedario y pasaron a ser dígrafos
options.why: la escritura no cambió; lo que cambió fue el inventario de letras.

options.text: Desaparecieron de la escritura del español
options.why: sigue escribiéndose *chocolate* y *llave* exactamente igual.

options.text: Empezaron a ordenarse dentro de la c y la l
options.why: eso ya se había decidido en 1994; 2010 sacó la conclusión.

niche.language.spanish.la-enie-casi-se-p.title: La letra que inventó la pereza y que Bruselas casi borra
niche.language.spanish.la-enie-casi-se-p.hook: La ñ nació como una trampa de copistas con prisa. En 1991 Bruselas estuvo a punto de borrarla por libre comercio.
niche.language.spanish.la-enie-casi-se-p.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Title reworded for grammar; the 1991 EEC keyboard dispute and the decree of 23 April 1993 check out.

niche.language.spanish.la-enie-casi-se-p.body:
La ñ empezó siendo un atajo. En los monasterios medievales el pergamino era caro y la mano se cansaba, así que la doble *nn* del latín —*annus*, *pannus*— se abreviaba escribiendo una sola *n* con una rayita encima. Esa rayita, la tilde, es literalmente una *n* aplastada.

El atajo se volvió sonido, y el sonido se volvió letra. Hoy la ñ no es solo española: la usan el gallego, el asturiano, el euskera, el aimara, el quechua y el guaraní. El inglés se la lleva prestada cada vez que escribe *jalapeño* o *El Niño*.

En 1991 casi desaparece de los teclados. Algunos fabricantes, con el respaldo de la Comunidad Económica Europea, argumentaron que obligar a incluir la ñ en los teclados vendidos en España era proteccionismo disfrazado y violaba la libre circulación de mercancías. España respondió el 23 de abril de 1993 con un real decreto que mantuvo la obligación.

Una raya que ahorraba tinta en el siglo XII terminó defendida como patrimonio cultural en un tribunal de comercio.

recall.question: ¿De dónde sale la tilde de la ñ?
recall.answer: De una abreviatura. Los copistas medievales escribían la doble *nn* latina como una sola *n* con una rayita encima para ahorrar espacio y esfuerzo; esa rayita es una *n* comprimida. Después el dígrafo abreviado se consolidó como letra propia.

niche.language.spanish.tres-maneras-de-d.title: Un país, tres segundas personas
niche.language.spanish.tres-maneras-de-d.hook: En Medellín te dicen vos, en Bogotá usted y en Cartagena tú. Los tres son restos de la misma pelea del siglo XVI.
niche.language.spanish.tres-maneras-de-d.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Fixed a tu/vos mix inside one clause ('uses ... venis').

niche.language.spanish.tres-maneras-de-d.body:
Colombia hace algo que casi ningún idioma tolera: usa tres pronombres distintos para hablarle a una sola persona, y el que uses delata de dónde vienes. Paisas, caldenses y caleños vosean. El altiplano bogotano ustedea incluso con los amigos y con el perro. La costa Caribe tutea.

El origen está en una inflación de cortesía. El latín *vos* era plural y servía para tratar con respeto a una sola persona; de tanto usarse, se gastó. España resolvió el desgaste con *vuestra merced* —que se comprimió hasta *usted*— y abandonó el *vos*. América no se enteró toda al tiempo: las regiones con tráfico constante hacia la metrópoli adoptaron el cambio; las lejanas conservaron el *vos* del siglo XVI.

Por eso el voseo no es una deformación: es la forma antigua, conservada en los lugares a los que la moda no llegó. Antioquia y el Valle hablan, en este punto, más parecido al español de Cervantes que Madrid.

Y la conjugación se conservó con él: *vos sos*, *vos tenés*, *vos cantás*, *vení*, *comé* — imperativos a los que solo se les cayó la *d* final de *venid* y *comed*.

recall.question: ¿Por qué el voseo aparece justo en las regiones más alejadas de los grandes centros coloniales?
recall.answer: Porque el voseo es la forma vieja, no una innovación. España sustituyó el *vos* por *tú* y *vuestra merced* (de donde sale *usted*), y el cambio viajó con el contacto: las zonas con tráfico constante hacia la metrópoli lo adoptaron, y las aisladas conservaron el *vos* del siglo XVI.

niche.language.untranslatable.the-word-e.title: There is no English word for the best part of lunch
niche.language.untranslatable.the-word-e.hook: English can describe sitting at the table long after the plates are cleared. It just needs a whole sentence to do it.
niche.language.untranslatable.the-word-e.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Hook's 'eleven words' did not count out; replaced.

niche.language.untranslatable.the-word-e.body:
*Sobremesa*: the stretch of time that starts when dessert is served and ends whenever the conversation does. Nobody stands up. Coffee appears, maybe an aguardiente. The meal is over and the table is not.

"Untranslatable" is an overstatement — that paragraph just translated it. What English lacks is a *single word*, a different and more interesting claim: languages hand short labels to whatever their speakers do often enough to need one.

The gap is not about concepts. It is about how long you sit there.

recall.question: What does a so-called "untranslatable" word usually mean?
recall.answer: Not that the idea cannot be expressed — almost anything can be paraphrased — but that the other language has no *single word* for it. Short labels get minted for what a culture does often, so lexical gaps map habits rather than thoughts.

niche.language.writing-systems.hangul-is.title: The alphabet that draws the inside of your mouth
niche.language.writing-systems.hangul-is.hook: Korean consonants are not arbitrary squiggles. Each one is a small drawing of what your tongue is doing.
niche.language.writing-systems.hangul-is.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.language.writing-systems.hangul-is.body:
Latin letters are the descendants of pictures of things — A was an ox head, once, upside down. They tell you nothing about the sound. Hangul does something no other major script does: the letter *is* a diagram of the organ making the noise.

Announced around 1443 and published in 1446 under Sejong the Great, its five basic consonants each depict an articulation. ㄱ shows the back of the tongue blocking the soft palate, which is exactly what you do to say *k*. ㅁ is a mouth, and it is *m*. ㄴ is the tongue tip touching behind the teeth, *n*. Then the system compounds: add a stroke for more breath, so ㄷ becomes ㅌ, plain *t* becoming aspirated *t*.

The companion volume, the *Hunminjeongeum Haerye*, explains all of this in writing — which makes Hangul one of the very few scripts in history whose designers left behind their reasoning.

Sejong's stated motive was blunt: Korean sounds do not fit Chinese characters, and ordinary people could not learn them. It was engineering aimed at literacy, and it worked.

recall.question: What makes Hangul's consonant letters unusual among the world's scripts?

options.text: They were derived from simplified Chinese characters
options.why: the *Haerye* explicitly grounds them in articulation instead.

options.text: Their shapes depict the position of the speech organs that produce them
options.why: ㅁ is a mouth, ㄱ is the tongue blocking the palate.

options.text: Each letter stands for a whole syllable
options.why: syllables are built by stacking letters into blocks, but the letters themselves are phonemes.

niche.language.writing-systems.the-man-w.title: A man who could not read invented a writing system
niche.language.writing-systems.the-man-w.hook: Sequoyah could not read a word of any language. He worked out what writing was from first principles, and then built one.
niche.language.writing-systems.the-man-w.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.language.writing-systems.the-man-w.body:
Every other script on Earth was adapted from an older script, or built by people who already knew how writing worked. The Cherokee syllabary is the exception that historians keep coming back to: Sequoyah was illiterate in every language, including his own, when he started.

He had seen white settlers reading — "talking leaves" — and reasoned from the outside that marks could hold speech. Through the late 1810s he tried a symbol per word, which failed under its own weight, then switched to a symbol per syllable. Cherokee has few enough syllables for that to work. He ended with 86 characters, later trimmed to 85 for the printing press.

The adoption is the astonishing part. By 1825 the majority of Cherokee could read and write in it, a language that had been unwritten a decade earlier. On 21 February 1828 the *Cherokee Phoenix* began publishing at New Echota in Cherokee and English, the first newspaper in a Native American language.

One man, working alone, compressed several thousand years of writing's development into about a decade.

recall.question: Why was a syllabary — rather than an alphabet — the right design for Cherokee?
recall.answer: Sequoyah first tried one symbol per word and drowned in symbols. Cherokee has a small enough inventory of syllables that one symbol per syllable is manageable: 86 characters covered the language, and learners could start reading almost immediately without analysing sounds below the syllable.

niche.music.theory-math.the-circle-does-.title: The circle of fifths is not a circle
niche.music.theory-math.the-circle-does-.hook: Go up twelve perfect fifths and you should land seven octaves higher. You land a quarter of a semitone past it.

series.title: Why the piano is a lie

niche.music.theory-math.the-circle-does-.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.music.theory-math.the-circle-does-.body:
Start on C and climb by perfect fifths — the interval that sounds most obviously *right* to a human ear, two strings vibrating at a clean 3:2. C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯, E♯, and the twelfth step lands you on B♯, which on a piano is the key marked C.

It is not the same C. Twelve fifths multiply out to $(3/2)^{12}=129.746\ldots$, while seven octaves are exactly $2^7=128$. You have overshot by a factor of 531441/524288, about 1.36%.

That sounds trivial. It is not: in musical units the gap is 23.46 cents, nearly a quarter of a semitone, and any competent listener hears it as out of tune. It is called the Pythagorean comma, and it has been the central embarrassment of Western music for 2,500 years.

You might hope it is a rounding artefact that a cleverer tuning would fix. It is not fixable, and the proof is one line.
niche.music.theory-math.the-circle-does-.rigor:
Suppose $m$ fifths equalled $n$ octaves exactly: $(3/2)^{m}=2^{n}$, so $3^{m}=2^{n+m}$. For $m\ge 1$ the left side is odd and the right even — contradiction. Equivalently, $\log_2(3/2)=0.5849625\ldots$ is irrational, so the fifths spiral forever and never revisit a pitch.

The only question left is which rational approximations are *good*, and continued fractions answer it exactly. The expansion $\log_2(3/2)=[0;1,1,2,2,3,1,5,2,\ldots]$ gives convergents

$$\tfrac11,\;\tfrac12,\;\tfrac35,\;\tfrac7{12},\;\tfrac{24}{41},\;\tfrac{31}{53}.$$

There is the twelve-note keyboard: $7/12$, the fourth convergent, meaning twelve equal steps put the fifth at 700 cents against a true 701.955. The next serious improvements are 41 and 53 notes to the octave — and 53-tone equal temperament really does have a famously pure fifth, 701.887 cents, wrong by seven hundredths of a cent.

Western music has twelve notes because a continued fraction has a large partial quotient in the right place. Nothing deeper.

So: 23.46 cents you cannot destroy. The only choice is where to put them — and that choice is the next three hundred years of music.

recall.question: Why can no tuning make a whole number of perfect fifths equal a whole number of octaves?

options.text: It would force $3^{m}=2^{n+m}$, which unique factorisation forbids
options.why: $\log_2(3/2)$ is irrational, so the spiral of fifths never closes.

options.text: Because human hearing is imprecise
options.why: the gap is an exact arithmetic fact, audible or not.

options.text: Because the octave is not exactly 2:1
options.why: the octave is exactly 2:1 by definition; the fifth is what gets bent.

niche.music.tuning.the-piano-is-out-of-t.title: The piano in tune is the piano lying evenly
niche.music.tuning.the-piano-is-out-of-t.hook: A perfectly tuned piano has no pure thirds, and its octaves are deliberately too wide.

series.title: Why the piano is a lie

niche.music.tuning.the-piano-is-out-of-t.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.music.tuning.the-piano-is-out-of-t.body:
The modern answer to the comma is to refuse to choose a victim. Make every semitone the same ratio, $\sqrt[12]{2}$, and the twelve fifths close by construction. Zhu Zaiyu worked out the number in China in 1584; Simon Stevin reached it in Europe around 1585.

The cost is paid by everybody, a little. Every fifth on your piano is about two cents flat of pure — imperceptible. Every major third is about fourteen cents *sharp*, which is very perceptible; if you have ever thought a piano chord sounds slightly harder than the same chord on a guitar or in a choir, that is what you are hearing. Equal temperament is not clean. It is uniformly slightly dirty, which turns out to be a much better product.

Then the second lie, which is physical rather than mathematical. Real piano strings are stiff steel, so they do not vibrate like ideal strings: their overtones come out sharp of the exact harmonics. Tuners tune by listening to overtones, so they stretch — treble progressively sharp, bass progressively flat. O. L. Railsback measured the resulting curve in the 1930s.

Which makes the closing accounting rather neat.
niche.music.tuning.the-piano-is-out-of-t.rigor:
Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve ratios of $2^{1/12}\approx 1.059463$, so every semitone is exactly 100 cents. The fifth is 700 cents against a just 701.955, and the major third is 400 against a just 386.314 — errors of $-1.96$ and $+13.69$ cents.

Look at that first number again. Episode 1's Pythagorean comma was 23.46 cents, and

$$\frac{23.46}{12}=1.955 .$$

Equal temperament is exactly the scheme that takes the comma and divides it by twelve, giving each fifth an equal share of the debt. That is the whole idea, in one division.

The stretch is a different beast. For a real string of stiffness $B$, the $n$th partial sits at $f_n\approx n f_1\sqrt{1+Bn^2}$ rather than $nf_1$. A tuner matching the second partial of a low note to the fundamental of the note an octave up is therefore matching something already sharp, so the octave comes out wider than 2:1 — and the error compounds across the keyboard.

So a correctly tuned piano is out of tune with the harmonic series twice: once on purpose, by arithmetic, and once on purpose, by physics.

recall.question: Why does a piano tuner deliberately stretch octaves beyond the exact 2:1 ratio?

options.text: To compensate for the Pythagorean comma
options.why: that is already handled by equal temperament, which divides it evenly among the fifths.

options.text: Because stiff strings have overtones sharp of the true harmonics
options.why: tuners match overtones, so an octave that sounds clean ends up wider than 2:1.

options.text: To make the instrument louder in the treble
options.why: stretch is about pitch, not amplitude.

options.text: Because listeners prefer sharp high notes for no physical reason
options.why: the reason is measurable string inharmonicity, not taste alone.

niche.music.tuning.where-to-hide-a-comma.title: Somewhere on your keyboard, a wolf is living
niche.music.tuning.where-to-hide-a-comma.hook: You cannot destroy the comma. You can only decide which chord has to carry it — and that decision picks which keys exist.

series.title: Why the piano is a lie

niche.music.tuning.where-to-hide-a-comma.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.music.tuning.where-to-hide-a-comma.body:
Twenty-three cents have to go somewhere. Pythagorean tuning makes the brutal choice: tune eleven fifths pure and shove the whole comma into the twelfth. That last interval beats violently, and was nicknamed the *wolf* for the howl. Play in the wrong key and the wolf is in your chord.

Renaissance musicians made a different trade. They cared less about fifths than about *thirds*, which Pythagorean tuning leaves badly sharp. Quarter-comma meantone flattens every fifth slightly so that the major thirds come out perfect at 5:4 — luminous, beatless triads, which is why Renaissance choral music sounds the way it does. The price: the leftover fifth is now even worse, and whole regions of the keyboard become unplayable. You composed in the keys that worked.

Around 1690 the well temperaments arrived: distribute the comma *unevenly*, so no interval is unbearable but every key keeps a flavour — C major bright, A♭ major dark. Bach's *Well-Tempered Clavier* (1722, 1742) walks through all twenty-four. Which tuning he meant is genuinely disputed.

The arithmetic of the trade-off is unforgiving.
niche.music.tuning.where-to-hide-a-comma.rigor:
Cents are logarithmic: an interval of ratio $r$ measures $1200\log_2 r$.

In quarter-comma meantone the fifth is tuned to $\sqrt[4]{5}:1$, so four fifths stacked and dropped two octaves give exactly $5/4$. In cents the fifth is $300\log_2 5=696.58$, flat of the pure 701.955 by 5.38 cents; four of them minus two octaves give exactly $386.31$ cents, the just major third.

Now the bill. A twelve-key octave forces the twelve fifths to total seven octaves, $8400$ cents. Eleven tempered fifths take $11\times 696.58=7662.4$, leaving

$$8400-7662.4=737.6\ \text{cents}$$

for the last one — about 36 cents wider than pure. That is the wolf, usually parked between G♯ and E♭ where a Renaissance composer would not go.

The general principle: the comma is conserved. Every scheme is a choice of how to distribute a fixed error budget of 23.46 cents across twelve fifths, and you are choosing which chords sound holy and which sound wrong.

Unless you refuse to choose, and spread it perfectly evenly — which is the modern answer, and which creates its own strange problem.

recall.question: What does quarter-comma meantone buy, and what does it pay?
recall.answer: It buys pure 5:4 major thirds by flattening each fifth to $\sqrt[4]{5}:1$ (696.58 cents, about 5.4 cents flat). It pays with a wolf fifth of roughly 737.6 cents left over, and with whole keys becoming unusable — which is why so much Renaissance music lives in so few keys.

niche.places.bogota.transmilenio.title: El metro que Bogotá construyó con buses
niche.places.bogota.transmilenio.hook: Bogotá resolvió su metro sin construir un metro: buses, pero con derechos de vía de tren.
niche.places.bogota.transmilenio.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.places.bogota.transmilenio.body:
La idea que volvió famosa a Bogotá en los congresos de urbanismo del mundo es casi una trampa de ingeniería: un bus cuesta una fracción de lo que cuesta un vagón, y lo que hace lento a un bus no es el bus sino el tráfico. Quítele el tráfico —carril exclusivo, estaciones cerradas con plataforma a la altura del piso, pago antes de subir, buses articulados— y tendrá un metro de superficie por una décima parte del precio.

No fue invención bogotana. Curitiba llevaba décadas haciéndolo, y Quito tenía su trolebús. Lo que hizo la administración de Enrique Peñalosa (1998-2000), que descartó los planes japoneses de metro subterráneo, fue construirlo a escala de capital. TransMilenio se inauguró el 4 de diciembre de 2000.

Hoy la red troncal pasa de 114 km con unas 139 estaciones y mueve del orden de 1,35 millones de pasajeros en un día hábil. También es, con enorme consistencia, la cosa de la que más se queja la ciudad: lleno, incómodo, víctima de su propio éxito.

Ambas cosas son ciertas a la vez, y eso mismo es la lección.

recall.question: ¿Cuál es el truco de ingeniería detrás de un sistema BRT como TransMilenio?
recall.answer: Que la lentitud de un bus la produce el tráfico, no el bus. Con carril exclusivo, estaciones cerradas, plataforma a nivel y pago previo, el bus alcanza capacidades de metro a una fracción del costo de obra.

niche.places.bogota.water-boils-at-ninet.title: In Bogotá, boiling water is not hot enough
niche.places.bogota.water-boils-at-ninet.hook: At 2,625 metres, a rolling boil is about nine degrees cooler than the one your recipe assumes.
niche.places.bogota.water-boils-at-ninet.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.places.bogota.water-boils-at-ninet.body:
The city sits at about 2,625 m, Monserrate another 500 m above it. Thinner air means water boils sooner: tables give 93.4 °C at 2,000 m and 90.0 °C at 3,000 m, leaving Bogotá near 91–92 °C.

Boiling is a ceiling, not a setting. A pot cannot get hotter than its boiling point, so beans that soften in forty minutes at sea level take far longer, and extra flame does nothing. Hence the pressure cooker: serious Andean equipment, not a gadget.

recall.question: Why does turning up the heat not fix slow cooking at altitude?
recall.answer: Because the water's temperature is pinned at its boiling point, which altitude has already lowered to about 91 °C. More flame boils it away faster; it does not make it hotter. Raising the pressure — a pressure cooker — is the only way to raise the ceiling.

niche.places.borders.the-land-nobody-wan.title: The only habitable place on Earth that nobody claims
niche.places.borders.the-land-nobody-wan.hook: Two countries, two border lines, and one patch of desert that each of them insists belongs to the other.
niche.places.borders.the-land-nobody-wan.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.places.borders.the-land-nobody-wan.body:
Britain drew the Egypt–Sudan border twice. The 1899 line cut straight along the 22nd parallel; the 1902 line followed where the tribes grazed. They swap two areas: the Hala'ib Triangle on the Red Sea, and Bir Tawil, 2,060 km² of desert.

Egypt insists on the 1899 line, Sudan on the 1902 one. Each version hands its claimant Hala'ib — and hands Bir Tawil to the other side. Claiming Bir Tawil would mean conceding Hala'ib, so nobody does, and it stays the one habitable place on Earth outside every state.

recall.question: Why would claiming Bir Tawil be a bad move for either Egypt or Sudan?
recall.answer: Because the two claims are a package. Each country's preferred border line simultaneously gives it the valuable Hala'ib Triangle and gives Bir Tawil away. Taking Bir Tawil means adopting the other country's line, which surrenders Hala'ib.

niche.places.borders.the-town-with-two-c.title: A border that goes through a front door, and then a shed
niche.places.borders.the-town-with-two-c.hook: One town, twenty-two Belgian exclaves, and seven Dutch enclaves inside those. The border runs through a front door.
niche.places.borders.the-town-with-two-c.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.places.borders.the-town-with-two-c.body:
Baarle is one town on the Dutch–Belgian frontier and two municipalities, and the map of it looks like someone spilled it. Baarle-Hertog, the Belgian side, consists of 26 separate parcels, 22 of them sitting entirely inside the Netherlands. Inside those Belgian islands there are seven Dutch islands — counter-enclaves — six of them within a single Belgian parcel.

Nobody designed this. It is sediment: centuries of medieval land deals, swaps and sales between the Lords of Breda and the Dukes of Brabant, each transaction recorded plot by plot, never tidied. When the Netherlands and Belgium finally drew a national border in the Treaty of Maastricht of 1843, they ratified the mess rather than rationalise it.

So the line runs through a furniture showroom, a shed, a barn and the loading dock of a liquor store. One house has the border through the middle of its front door and carries two addresses: Loveren 2, Baarle-Hertog and Loveren 19, Baarle-Nassau.

It is what a border looks like when it is inherited instead of drawn.

recall.question: What is a counter-enclave, as found in Baarle?

options.text: A piece of one country entirely surrounded by an exclave of another
options.why: Baarle has Dutch parcels inside Belgian parcels inside the Netherlands.

options.text: A border town governed jointly by two states
options.why: Baarle has two separate municipalities with two administrations, not one shared one.

options.text: A territory claimed by two countries at once
options.why: the Baarle parcels are undisputed; each one has a settled owner.

niche.places.maps-projections.how-many-g.title: How many Greenlands fit inside Africa?
niche.places.maps-projections.how-many-g.hook: On the wall map they look the same size. Commit to a number before you read on.
niche.places.maps-projections.how-many-g.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.places.maps-projections.how-many-g.body:
Picture the world map that hung in your classroom. Greenland is an enormous white slab across the top, comfortably the size of the African continent below it.

Now commit to a number. Africa's area divided by Greenland's: is it about 1? About 3? About 8? Bigger?

While you decide, the politics. In 1855 the Scottish clergyman James Gall described an equal-area projection that nobody noticed. In 1967 the German historian Arno Peters independently arrived at essentially the same map and, from 1973, promoted it hard as the anti-colonial correction to Mercator — the map that finally gives the global South its true size.

Cartographers were furious, partly because Peters claimed properties his map did not have, and partly because equal-area projections had been sitting on the shelf for a century. The fight got so tiresome that in 1989 seven North American geographic organisations adopted a joint resolution asking everyone to stop using *any* rectangular world map.

Both sides were right about something. Your number first.

recall.question: How many times larger than Greenland is Africa in reality?
recall.answer: About fourteen. Greenland is roughly 2.2 million km², Africa roughly 30 million. On Mercator they look comparable because Greenland sits almost entirely above 60° N, where the projection multiplies area by four or more, while Africa sits on the equator, where it multiplies by one.

niche.places.maps-projections.mercator-w.title: Greenland is not the size of Africa, and Mercator knew
niche.places.maps-projections.mercator-w.hook: Mercator's map is not a bad picture of the world. It is a very good picture of a compass bearing.
niche.places.maps-projections.mercator-w.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Added the reciprocal related link to the Greenland challenge card.

niche.places.maps-projections.mercator-w.body:
Gerardus Mercator published his world map in 1569 with a title that gives away the whole game: *…ad Usum Navigantium*, for the use of navigators. He was not trying to show you how big places are. He was solving one problem: make a course of constant compass bearing come out as a straight line you can rule on the chart.

That problem has exactly one solution, and the solution demands the distortion. To keep angles right, the map has to stretch north–south by exactly as much as it has already stretched east–west — and near the poles that is a lot. Greenland ends up looking the size of Africa, which has about fourteen times the area.

So the familiar complaint is aimed at the wrong target. A Mercator map on a ship's table is a precision instrument. The same map on a classroom wall, where nobody is plotting a course and everybody is comparing continents, is a category error that has been repeated for four centuries.

The stretching factor is worth deriving, because it explains the whole thing.
niche.places.maps-projections.mercator-w.rigor:
A parallel at latitude $\varphi$ has true length $2\pi R\cos\varphi$, but on a rectangular map it is drawn the full width. So the east–west scale factor is $\sec\varphi$.

Conformality — angles preserved — requires the north–south scale to match it at every point. That forces

$$\frac{dy}{d\varphi}=\sec\varphi \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y(\varphi)=\ln\!\left|\tan\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\tfrac{\varphi}{2}\right)\right| ,$$

the Mercator ordinate, and a divergence at $\varphi\to\pm 90^{\circ}$: the poles are infinitely far up the page, which is why no Mercator map shows them.

Area scales as the product of the two factors:

$$\text{area factor}=\sec^{2}\varphi .$$

At $30^{\circ}$ that is $1.33$. At $60^{\circ}$ it is exactly $4$. At $75^{\circ}$ it is about $15$. Greenland lies almost entirely north of $60^{\circ}$ and Africa straddles the equator, so the two are being drawn on wildly different scales in the same picture. Nothing is wrong with the map; the reader is just using it for a question it was never asked.

recall.question: Why must a map that turns constant compass bearings into straight lines inflate the polar regions?

options.text: Keeping angles correct forces the north–south stretch to equal the east–west stretch $\sec\varphi$, so areas grow as $\sec^{2}\varphi$
options.why: unbounded as you approach the poles.

options.text: Because the Earth is an oblate spheroid rather than a sphere
options.why: a real but tiny effect, nothing like the polar inflation.

options.text: Because paper is rectangular and the Earth is not
options.why: many rectangular projections preserve area; the inflation comes from conformality specifically.

niche.weird.coincidences.remember-counti.title: Remember counting the complement? It explains why coincidences are boring.
niche.weird.coincidences.remember-counti.hook: Twenty-three people in a room, and the odds of a shared birthday are better than even. Count pairs, not people.
niche.weird.coincidences.remember-counti.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Absorbed the 253-people / 253-pairs coincidence from a rejected near-duplicate fact card.

niche.weird.coincidences.remember-counti.body:
The first real trick you learn in probability is to compute what you want by computing its opposite: *at least one* is impossible to count directly, *none* is easy. The birthday problem is that trick's greatest hit, and it is also a general theory of coincidence.

Ask 23 strangers their birthdays and the chance two of them match is 50.7%. People find this absurd, and the reason they find it absurd is that they are silently asking a different question — *does anyone share mine?* — which involves 22 comparisons. The actual question involves every pair: $\binom{23}{2}=253$ of them.

That is the whole lesson, and it generalises well past birthdays. A "miracle" is almost always an *at-least-one* event that your intuition has priced as a *this-specific-one* event. In a country of 50 million, things with a one-in-a-million chance happen to fifty people every time the clock ticks.

The arithmetic is short enough to do completely.
niche.weird.coincidences.remember-counti.rigor:
With $n$ people and $d=365$ equally likely birthdays, compute the complement:

$$\bar{p}(n)=\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{d}\right),\qquad p(n)=1-\bar{p}(n).$$

Take logs and use $\ln(1-x)\approx -x$:

$$\ln\bar{p}(n)\approx-\frac{1}{d}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k=-\frac{n(n-1)}{2d},$$

so $p(n)\approx 1-e^{-n(n-1)/730}$. The exponent is quadratic in $n$, which is the entire surprise: doubling the room quadruples the collisions.

$p(23)=0.507$, $p(57)\approx 0.99$, $p(70)\approx 0.999$. Ask instead *does anyone share mine?* and you need 253 people for even odds — the same 253 as the pair count above, for no reason whatsoever.

Setting $p=1/2$ gives $n\approx 1.177\sqrt{d}$, and that square root is why cryptographers care: a hash with $N$ output bits has $d=2^{N}$ values, so collisions appear after about $2^{N/2}$ hashes, not $2^{N}$. A 128-bit hash gives 64 bits of collision resistance. The birthday attack is this card, with $d$ made enormous.

recall.question: Why do people underestimate the chance of a shared birthday in a room of 23?

options.text: They forget about leap years
options.why: 29 February changes the answer by a negligible amount.

options.text: They picture comparisons with themselves (22 of them) instead of all pairs (253)
options.why: the number of pairs grows quadratically, and that is where the probability comes from.

options.text: They assume birthdays are uniformly distributed
options.why: real birthdays are slightly clumped, which makes matches *more* likely, not less.

niche.weird.eccentrics.another-roof-anot.title: He arrived at your door and said your brain was open
niche.weird.eccentrics.another-roof-anot.hook: No house, no job, no possessions beyond a suitcase — and roughly 1,500 papers with more than 500 co-authors.
niche.weird.eccentrics.another-roof-anot.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.weird.eccentrics.another-roof-anot.body:
Paul Erdős (1913–1996) did mathematics the way other people are homeless. He owned a suitcase. He would appear at a colleague's house, work for a few days on whatever problem was in the air, and move on — "another roof, another proof". The lifestyle was not a quirk attached to the work; it *was* the work. Mathematics, for him, was a conversation you had to keep physically walking towards.

The output is barely believable: around 1,525 papers, more than any mathematician in history, with over 500 collaborators. That number is why the Erdős number exists — your collaboration distance from him, which several hundred thousand mathematicians can compute for themselves.

He had a private vocabulary for everything. God was the SF, the Supreme Fascist, who kept a Book containing the perfect proof of every theorem; the best compliment Erdős could pay an argument was that it came straight from the Book. Children were epsilons.

Paul Hoffman's 1998 biography calls him *The Man Who Loved Only Numbers*, which is almost right. What he loved was doing numbers *with* someone.

recall.question: What is an Erdős number, and why does the concept exist for him and not for other mathematicians?
recall.answer: It is your collaboration distance from Paul Erdős — 1 if you co-authored with him, 2 if you co-authored with one of his co-authors, and so on. It exists because with over 500 collaborators and around 1,525 papers he sits at the centre of the mathematical collaboration graph.

niche.weird.eccentrics.grothendieck-aske.title: He rebuilt geometry, then spent forty years walking away from it
niche.weird.eccentrics.grothendieck-aske.hook: In 2010 the greatest geometer of the century wrote to demand that his own work be removed from every library.
niche.weird.eccentrics.grothendieck-aske.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.weird.eccentrics.grothendieck-aske.body:
Alexander Grothendieck (1928–2014) arrived at the IHÉS in 1958 and, over twelve years, rewrote algebraic geometry from the ground up — schemes, sheaf cohomology, the machinery that most of modern arithmetic geometry still runs on. Then, in 1970, he discovered the institute was partly funded by the military, and left.

He never really came back. In 1988 he refused the Crafoord Prize in an open letter, arguing that established mathematicians did not need more money and that the ethics of the scientific community were in decline. In 1991 he moved to Lasserre, a village in the Pyrenees, and gave his address to nobody.

The last act is the strangest. In January 2010 he wrote a *Déclaration d'intention de non-publication*: everything of his in circulation had been published without his permission, and he wanted all of it withdrawn — from libraries, from the web, everywhere.

It could not be done, of course. A mathematician's real work is in other people's heads, and there is no recall procedure for that. His refusal was total and, by construction, impossible.

recall.question: What did Grothendieck's 2010 declaration ask for?

options.text: That his prizes be returned
options.why: the prize he refused was the Crafoord, in 1988, a separate act.

options.text: That his published work be withdrawn from libraries and the internet
options.why: he claimed it had all been published without his permission.

options.text: That his students stop citing him
options.why: the declaration targeted publication and distribution, not citation.

niche.weird.eccentrics.the-prize-he-woul.title: The Poincaré conjecture was solved on a preprint server
niche.weird.eccentrics.the-prize-he-woul.hook: He solved a hundred-year-old problem, posted it for free, and turned down a million dollars and the Fields Medal.
niche.weird.eccentrics.the-prize-he-woul.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.weird.eccentrics.the-prize-he-woul.body:
No journal. No press conference. Between November 2002 and July 2003, Grigori Perelman posted three preprints to arXiv, and buried inside them was the proof of the Poincaré conjecture — open since 1904, and the only one of the seven Millennium Problems that has been solved.

Then he began refusing things. He resigned from the Steklov Institute in December 2005. In 2006 he was awarded the Fields Medal and declined it, the only person ever to do so. In March 2010 the Clay Mathematics Institute awarded him its million-dollar prize; on 1 July he turned that down too.

His stated reason was not modesty. It was a judgement about the community: he considered the decision unjust because it did not recognise Richard Hamilton, whose Ricci flow programme the proof completes, and he had lost patience with a field whose ethical standards he thought had slipped.

Whatever you make of the refusals, one consequence is concrete. The single most valuable piece of mathematics of the century sits on a public server, free, with no publisher between it and you.

recall.question: What reason did Perelman give for declining the Millennium Prize in 2010?
recall.answer: Not humility. He said his disagreement was with the organised mathematical community and that he considered its decisions unjust — in particular that Richard Hamilton, whose Ricci flow programme the proof completes, was not recognised alongside him.

niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.bunga-bunga.title: Virginia Woolf, in a false beard, inspecting the Royal Navy
niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.bunga-bunga.hook: Six people in fancy dress talked their way onto Britain's most secret warship, speaking a language they invented on the train.
niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.bunga-bunga.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.bunga-bunga.body:
On 7 February 1910, six people in turbans and darkened skin were received aboard HMS *Dreadnought*, the most advanced and most secret warship in the world, as a delegation of Abyssinian royalty. The Royal Navy gave them a full ceremonial reception.

The visitors were Horace de Vere Cole and friends, among them the 28-year-old Virginia Stephen — later Virginia Woolf — in a false beard. Their costumes came from a theatrical outfitter. Their language was gibberish improvised from scraps of Latin and Greek. They asked for prayer mats and tried to award fake military honours to the officers, who accepted them.

The press reported that the delegation kept exclaiming *bunga bunga*. The phrase stuck to the ship for years; when *Dreadnought* rammed a German submarine in 1915, someone sent a congratulatory telegram reading only: BUNGA BUNGA.

A hoax survives on confidence, not on plausibility. Nobody checked, because nobody could imagine anyone daring.

niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.sokal-on-his-o.title: "Intellectually lazy"
niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.sokal-on-his-o.hook: A physicist wrote nonsense about quantum gravity, got it published, and then explained why he had done it.
niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.sokal-on-his-o.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.sokal-on-his-o.body:
In May 1996 *Social Text* ran "Transgressing the Boundaries: Towards a Transformative Hermeneutics of Quantum Gravity". Three weeks later its author, the NYU physicist Alan Sokal, revealed in *Lingua Franca* that it was nonsense, written in the vocabulary the editors liked.

> The results of my little experiment demonstrate, at the very least, that some fashionable sectors of the American academic Left have been getting intellectually lazy.

The journal was not peer-reviewed then, which both sides still argue about. His sharpest point survives it: flattery is a hole in every filter.

niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.the-giant-that.title: The forgery of a forgery outsold the original
niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.the-giant-that.hook: A fake stone giant earned its maker a fortune. Then a fake of the fake earned more, and both drew queues.
niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.the-giant-that.author: author-sports-niche-1

reviewed.notes: Hull's argument was at a Methodist revival meeting, not with his cousin; inflation figure corrected.

niche.weird.hoaxes-frauds.the-giant-that.body:
On 16 October 1869, well-diggers behind a barn in Cardiff, New York, hit a three-metre stone man weighing nearly 1,400 kg. Crowds came at fifty cents a head, three to five hundred a day, to see a petrified biblical giant.

George Hull had carved it from Iowa gypsum and buried it the year before, at a cost of about \$2,600. He sold his share for \$23,000 — close to \$600,000 today — after losing an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about whether giants had really walked the Earth.

Then the part nobody plans. P. T. Barnum offered \$50,000, was refused, and simply had a copy made in plaster. He displayed the copy, in New York, while the original was also on show in New York. It is here that a rival exhibitor, David Hannum, is said to have complained that there's a sucker born every minute — a line that has been attached to Barnum ever since, and that Barnum appears not to have said.

Two men made fortunes from the same lie, and only one of them had to dig a hole.

recall.question: Who is actually credited with saying "there's a sucker born every minute", and about what?
recall.answer: David Hannum, a rival showman, reportedly said it about the crowds paying to see *Barnum's plaster copy* of the Cardiff Giant — a fake of a fake. The line is almost universally misattributed to Barnum himself.

niche.weird.lost-things.alexandria-did-n.title: Nobody burned the Library of Alexandria
niche.weird.lost-things.alexandria-did-n.hook: The great fire that destroyed the Library of Alexandria is the tidiest story in ancient history, and probably did not happen.
niche.weird.lost-things.alexandria-did-n.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.weird.lost-things.alexandria-did-n.body:
The story wants a villain. Caesar in 48 BC, or a Christian mob in 391, or the Arab conquest of 642 — pick your culprit and the greatest collection of antiquity goes up in one afternoon, taking the ancient world's knowledge with it.

The evidence does not cooperate. Caesar's fire seems to have reached warehouses near the docks, not the main collection: the Library is attested afterwards. The Serapeum, destroyed in 391, may well have held no significant books by then. The 642 story appears in sources written centuries later and is treated with deep suspicion.

What actually happened is duller and much worse. In 145 BC Ptolemy VIII expelled foreign scholars from Alexandria and they scattered across the eastern Mediterranean. The institution's prestige went with them. Funding declined. Appointments became political. The city was fought over repeatedly — Aurelian's forces wrecked the very quarter where the Library stood in the 270s AD.

So there was no afternoon. There were three hundred years of nobody quite paying for it any more. Which is the version worth remembering, because it is the version that can happen to you.

recall.question: What is the best-supported account of how the Library of Alexandria was lost?

options.text: Julius Caesar burned it in 48 BC
options.why: his fire appears to have hit dockside warehouses, and the Library is attested in later sources.

options.text: A gradual institutional decline over centuries
options.why: expelled scholars from 145 BC, lost funding and prestige, and repeated destruction of the quarter it stood in.

options.text: The Arab conquest destroyed it in 642 AD
options.why: that account first appears centuries after the event and historians treat it sceptically.

niche.weird.lost-things.the-machine-that.title: Fifteen hundred years ahead of schedule, then dropped in the sea
niche.weird.lost-things.the-machine-that.hook: A lump of corroded bronze from a Roman-era shipwreck turned out to contain thirty gears and an eclipse calendar.
niche.weird.lost-things.the-machine-that.author: author-sports-niche-1
niche.weird.lost-things.the-machine-that.body:
Sponge divers working a wreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in 1901 brought up statues, coins, and a shoebox-sized lump of corroded bronze that sat in a museum drawer while people argued about what it was.

It is a geared astronomical computer. Built in the late second or early first century BC, it carried some 35 meshing bronze gears, 30 of them still visible. Turn a crank and it gave the positions of the Sun and Moon through the zodiac, predicted eclipses decades ahead, tracked the Metonic cycle, and displayed the four-year cycle of athletic games. One gear train models the Moon's *irregular* orbit with an off-centre pin-and-slot.

Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity is known in Europe again until the astronomical clocks of the fourteenth century.

The unnerving part is not that the Greeks could do this. It is that we have exactly one of them. Whatever tradition produced it left no other surviving machine, which means our picture of ancient technology is drawn from a sample of one that happened to sink in the right place.

recall.question: Why does the Antikythera mechanism unsettle historians of technology rather than just impress them?
recall.answer: Because it is a sample of one. A device with 30-plus gears modelling the Moon's irregular motion cannot have been a first attempt, yet no comparable machine survives from antiquity — and nothing of that complexity appears again in Europe until the fourteenth century. What else existed, we have no way of knowing.
